- Current health concerns and risk factors:  3 days of diarrhea with frequent urgency/tenesmus, infra-umbilical crampy abdominal pain (improves after bowel movements), nausea with one episode of vomiting after fruit this morning; no visible blood in stool; uncertain fever (reports sweating, no measured temp); mild abdominal tenderness with self-palpation; reduced oral intake and likely low fluid intake; unable to work due to symptoms. Asthma history. Family history of bowel cancer in father raises colorectal cancer risk (patient expressed concern).

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key findings: Acute onset (3 days) diarrhea with crampy lower abdominal pain, urgency/tenesmus, mild nausea and one emesis; no hematochezia; uncertain fever; mild tenderness; suboptimal hydration. Past history of asthma; father with colorectal cancer.
- Impression: Most consistent with acute gastroenteritis (viral > bacterial) based on acute self-limited course, lack of blood or high fever, and GI symptoms. Inhaler brand change unlikely cause (per clinician and DDx).
- Differentials (consistent with DDx and transcript):
  - Acute viral gastroenteritis – high likelihood.
  - Acute bacterial gastroenteritis/foodborne illness – moderate likelihood (less likely without fever/blood).
  - IBS-D – low likelihood given acute presentation.
  - Inflammatory bowel disease – low likelihood (no blood/chronicity).
  - Colorectal cancer – low likelihood as cause of this acute illness; family history noted as a long-term risk factor.
- Working diagnosis: Acute gastroenteritis.
- Management priorities: Hydration; symptom monitoring for fever or deterioration; temporary home rest/isolation; avoid unnecessary antibiotics; in-person assessment if worsening or not improving.

Management Plan

- Advice provided:
  - Increase oral fluids to prevent dehydration.
  - Monitor for fever; watch for worsening symptoms.
  - Stay home and rest until improvement.
  - Antibiotics not recommended for typical gastroenteritis.
  - Seek in-person GP review if symptoms worsen or do not improve; in-person abdominal exam if needed.
- Follow-up: Patient to monitor for 1–2 days and book in-person GP if not improving or if worsening.
- Patient education: Reassured that current symptoms are more consistent with infection rather than hereditary bowel cancer; long-term risk due to family history acknowledged for future preventive care.

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits):  Not recorded.
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral:  Not recorded.
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support):  Not recorded.
- CTG registration:  Not recorded.
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test):  Not recorded.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Acute viral gastroenteritis – Likelihood: High. Justification: Acute 3-day course, nausea/vomiting, crampy infra-umbilical pain relieved by bowel movements, no blood or high fever.
- Acute bacterial gastroenteritis (foodborne) – Likelihood: Moderate. Justification: Overlapping presentation with infectious colitis; absence of blood/high fever lowers probability.
- Irritable bowel syndrome, diarrhea predominant (IBS-D) – Likelihood: Low. Justification: Pain relief with defecation and urgency could fit, but acute onset and associated vomiting favor infection.

Quality checks
- Missing elements: Vitals (BP, pulse, temperature), BMI/anthropometrics, immunization review, comprehensive medication list (including dose/route/frequency), allergy confirmation documentation, alcohol/tobacco/substance history, sexual and reproductive health history, mental health screening (PHQ-9/GAD-7), oral/ear/vision exams, urinalysis, preventive screening status (e.g., colorectal screening plan given family history).
- Internal contradictions: Demographics conflict noted between stated DOB (1992 then 1990) and stated age 48; clarification needed.
- Transcript quality: Some speech was unclear with interruptions; limited objective data due to telehealth format and lack of vitals/exam.
